lines.text: The phone rings in the accounting department. It's the CEO.

lines: The voice is exactly right: the accent, the pauses, the way he says your name.
He needs help with a confidential deal, and a lawyer from a big London firm will call with the details.

lines.text: The money is wired. Millions of dollars, gone in minutes.
The CEO never called. According to US prosecutors, the voice was made by artificial intelligence.
And it allegedly happened again, and again, at thousands of companies around the world, for about 129 million dollars.
lines.say: And it allegedly happened again, and again, at thousands of companies around the world. For about 129 million dollars.

lines: Not long ago, faking someone's voice took a skilled impressionist. Now, with AI, a short recording can be enough.
Think of a parrot. It doesn't understand a word, but it can sound exactly like you.
Bosses are easy to record. They give interviews, earnings calls and conference talks.
In 2019, criminals cloned the voice of an energy company's boss and talked a manager into sending about 243,000 dollars.

lines.text: In 2024, a worker at the engineering firm Arup in Hong Kong joined a video call with what looked like senior colleagues. Every person on the call was a deepfake. The company lost about 25 million dollars.
lines.say: In 2024, a worker at the engineering firm Arrup in Hong Kong joined a video call with what looked like senior colleagues. Every person on the call was a deepfake. The company lost about 25 million dollars.

lines: In November 2026, prosecutors in New York unsealed charges against three men. They say the scheme ran from July 2024 to February 2026.
First, an email that seemed to come from the company's CEO, asking for help with a secret transaction.
Then a call, with the CEO's voice, and sometimes his face, made with AI.
Then the CEO handed over to a "lawyer" at a major international law firm. The lawyer was fake too.

lines.text: Prosecutors say one of the men, Jacob Soall, mostly played British lawyers, and kept a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call".
lines.say: Prosecutors say one of the men, Jacob Sole, mostly played British lawyers, and kept a handwritten script, titled, Lawyer Call.

lines: The lawyer gave the bank details. The employee sent the money.
Prosecutors say thousands of companies were targeted.
A hospital system in Missouri lost about 4.8 million dollars. A financial technology company in the UK lost about 11.6 million.
A hospital system in California, a bank in Rhode Island, a mutual fund company in Massachusetts, and even a pet food company in Florida were also named.

The money was sent to bank accounts in Spain, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore and China.
Then, prosecutors say, it was turned into cryptocurrency to hide where it came from, and split between the members of the group.

lines.text: Two of the men, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit, are accused of laundering the money.
lines.say: Two of the men, Sharon Hazzan and Guy Sheetreet, are accused of laundering the money.

lines.text: According to the indictment, Hazan boasted of laundering more than 400 million dollars in three years, and of being "number one all over the world".
lines.say: According to the indictment, Hazzan boasted of laundering more than 400 million dollars in three years, and of being, number one, all over the world.

lines.text: The men also allegedly used nicknames: "Rocky Balboa", "Superman Cash" and "Fat Boy".
lines.say: The men also allegedly used nicknames. Rocky Balboa. Superman Cash. And Fat Boy.

lines.text: Soall was arrested in Spain in June 2026. Hazan was arrested in Spain in August. Sheetrit was arrested in the UK in September.
lines.say: Sole was arrested in Spain in June 2026. Hazzan was arrested in Spain in August. Sheetreet was arrested in the U.K. in September.

lines: They face charges including wire fraud, money laundering and aggravated identity theft. The most serious counts carry up to 20 years in prison.
The United States has asked for all three to be extradited. They are presumed innocent, and their lawyers did not comment.

lines.text: Prosecutors and the FBI say criminals are learning to "weaponize" new technology faster than companies can keep up.
lines.say: Prosecutors and the F.B.I. say criminals are learning to weaponize new technology faster than companies can keep up.

lines: The defences are simple. Hang up, and call back on a number you already know. Use a code word. Never let one person send a big payment alone.
And be careful when a request is both urgent and secret. That is the oldest trick in the book.

lines.text: The voices were perfect. The faces looked real.
The only thing missing was the real boss.
